html:
The Pyrrhic War was fought from 280 to 275 BCE between Pyrrhus, king of Epirus in northwest Greece, and the Roman Republic, mostly in southern Italy and Sicily. It gave us the phrase "Pyrrhic victory".

The rich Greek city of Tarentum clashed with Rome and called on Pyrrhus, a cousin of Alexander and one of the best generals of his time, to help. He landed with a professional army and war elephants, beasts the Romans had never faced.

  • At Heraclea in 280 BCE and Asculum in 279 BCE he beat the Romans, but lost so many of his own men that, the story goes, he said one more such victory would ruin him.
  • Rome refused to make peace; the old blind Appius Claudius is said to have shamed the Senate out of it.
  • Pyrrhus then spent three years in Sicily fighting Carthage, without lasting success.
  • Back in Italy he fought the Romans at Beneventum in 275 BCE and then went home.

Tarentum surrendered in 272 BCE, and Rome now ruled all of Italy south of the Po valley. Its next war, with Carthage, was the First Punic War.
